meta.description: Gary Player said a version of it — but not this wording, and he did not coin it. The line is documented in 1961, and Player's own 1962 book credited Jerry Barber.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The more I practice, the luckier I get'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Gary Player, but he said "the harder I practice" and was quoting older golf folklore. Documented in 1961; Player credited Jerry Barber in 1962.

answer.label: Not coined by Gary Player — an older saying he made famous
answer.authorDates: b. 1 November 1935 · South African golfer, nine-time major champion
answer.sourceLine: Player is genuinely on record with a version of this line — but the wording he actually used was “The harder I practice, the luckier I get,” quoted by Guy Yocom in Golf Digest (October 2002). Quote Investigator ↗ found the saying circulating long before that: the exact popular wording “the more I practice, the luckier I get” appears in a 1961 book, and Player’s own 1962 book credits the line to fellow golfer Jerry Barber.
answer.confidenceText: Player really did say a version of this — but he did not originate it, and the popular wording is not his.

source.rightsNote: No public-domain claim is possible here: the popular wording cannot be tied to any pre-1931 work. Its earliest documented appearance is a 1961 book, Player’s own retelling is in a 1962 book, and his quoted variant comes from a 2002 magazine article — all three texts are in copyright to their authors and publishers, while the underlying proverb has no identifiable author to hold rights in it.

author.name: Gary Player
author.heading: About Gary Player
author.metaLine: b. 1935 · South African golfer · nine major championships, career Grand Slam
author.bio: Gary Player was born in Johannesburg on 1 November 1935 and became one of the most travelled and most decorated golfers in the game’s history, winning nine major championships and completing the career Grand Slam in 1965 — the first non-American to do so. Nicknamed the Black Knight, he built a public identity around fitness and relentless practice, which is exactly why a practice-and-luck aphorism stuck to his name so firmly. He did use a version of the line in print, but he was quoting a piece of golf-world folk wisdom, not minting it.

Earlier credit by Player himself to Jerry Barber: Gary Player, Gary Player’s Golf Secrets (Englewood Cliffs, NJ: Prentice-Hall, 1962).

misattribution.heading: How it landed on Gary Player
misattribution.intro: This is a proverb with a long tail, not a quotation with an author. At least four golfers and several businessmen have been credited with it, and the wording shifts between “practice,” “work” and “know” depending on who is telling it.

items.why: Player is genuinely quoted saying “The harder I practice, the luckier I get” in Golf Digest, October 2002, and told an origin story about holing three bunker shots in a row in Texas. But Wikiquote’s own sourced entry ↗ appends the warning that the quote was probably not coined by him — and the “more I practice” wording usually put in his mouth is not the one he is documented using.
In Gary Player’s Golf Secrets (Prentice-Hall, 1962), Player tells a bunker-practice anecdote in which Barber — not Player — delivers the line. Quote Investigator ↗ quotes the passage.

Quote Investigator’s earliest located instance of the exact popular wording appears in this 1961 book, in a dialogue where a character says the shot was lucky and gets the reply “the more I practice, the luckier I get” — nothing to do with golf. See QI ↗.
Quote Investigator cites the Charleston Daily Mail in 1966 quoting Casper: “the more I practice, the luckier I get.” The saying was clearly common currency on tour by then. See QI ↗.

“I am a great believer in luck. The harder I work, the more of it I seem to have” — sourced on Wikiquote ↗, which also notes the shortened variant is sometimes mistakenly given to Thomas Jefferson, Stephen Leacock or Samuel Goldwyn.

misattribution.truthLine: Gary Player said a version of it and made it famous; he did not invent it. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes he “probably did not craft the aphorism,” which is documented in 1961 or earlier, with work-and-luck versions running back to 1949 and knowledge-and-luck versions to 1896.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Player
lead: Gary Player built his whole public persona on out-working everyone else — fitness regimes, endless bunker practice, a reputation for grinding. A one-line aphorism about practice manufacturing luck fits him so neatly that it migrated onto his name and stayed there, even though the saying was already in circulation when he was still winning his first majors.

The deeper problem is that this is a family of proverbs, not a single quotation. Quote Investigator tracks versions swapping “work” for “practice” and “know” for both, running back through the 1949 newspaper columns to the nineteenth century. Once a saying is that diffuse, whoever says it most memorably on television ends up owning it.
detailsBody: The wording Player is actually documented using is “The harder I practice, the luckier I get,” quoted by Guy Yocom in Golf Digest, October 2002 — the citation Wikiquote ↗ uses, alongside its own warning that the line was probably not coined by him.

A close cousin of the saying is separately sourced to Coleman Cox in Listen to This (1922): “I am a great believer in luck. The harder I work, the more of it I seem to have” — a line Wikiquote notes is sometimes mistakenly pinned on Thomas Jefferson, Stephen Leacock or Samuel Goldwyn.
context.pull: He said a version of it. He did not invent it — and the wording everyone quotes is not his.
